items.title: Padrastro
items.summary: You were my second father. You found dirt in your shoe and thanked it. You talked in affirmations so we went to parties underdressed. Mami sent a video of you once, thumping a tambora, And it got me through two weeks on the other side of Earth. That’s you driving five hours. With you I never took the bus alone. You bought a newsboy hat to look like Juan Luis Guerra one spring, And when the bro made so much fun of you at an Einstein Bros. Bagels, You ruffled, stood up, and threw it in the trash. My greetings passed through you and became songs. Kitchen counters feared you’d turn them into salsa beats. You got the water during every movie; no one was lonely on your watch. The word for it is stepfather But who’s to say if up or down. In Spanish it means “hangnail” too, But you know Mami, too proud, Won’t bite no nail about it. Now that you’re elsewhere, Though here in New York, I prefer to think of you As my father-on-loan: Wondering if you bought a new hat for the snowtime, And if so, well, what lucky years they were, Your interest in me.

items.title: The most important question you’ll ask 1,000 times a day
items.summary: You are able to make good decisions about how to live your life. I hate to open a new newsletter with a twee self-help aphorism covered in fortune cookie crumbs, but it’s probably the most important thing to start with. Because Epicureanism is an ancient Greek philosophy, and like almost all its contemporaries, it places responsibility on you . You are the overseer of your life. You can think things through, make good choices, and get things right. You are not some child, carried about by adult hands, blinking at a world blurring by. In the eyes of Greek philosophers, you are a rational, intelligent, deliberative human being. You control your life. Epicureanism argues that a good life is one where we develop strategies to either cure or endure pain — both physical and emotional — while seeking out opportunities to enjoy ourselves more. It says that a happy life means savoring simple pleasures where you are, right now, and with the people who matter. But to do that, we need to make better decisions. We need to willfully choose an Epicurean life. We need to work at happiness. Some of you might be wondering why there’s a cute little crab scuttling along our freshly minted logo. Well, that’s a hermit crab. In my upcoming book, The Art of Enough , I use the hermit crab motif to represent one of the most important ideas in Epicureanism. Because I think it embodies a certain skill we all need to nurture if we are to live a good life. This article is for Big Think members only. Become a member to read it in full. items.title: The Rise and Fall of the Telephone Century
items.summary: High-tech gadgets proliferated almost as rapidly in Mark Twain’s time as they do in ours, and he prided himself on being an early adopter. So when Alexander Graham Bell’s new telephone company began to offer service in Hartford, Connecticut, in 1877, Twain signed up, boasting (incorrectly) that his was the first line “ever used in a private house in the world.” Shortly afterward, he did set a record, becoming “the first author to deploy the telephone in fiction, in a peculiar story for The Atlantic Monthly ,” James Gleick writes in The Telephone: A New History . The comedy of “ The Loves of Alonzo Fitz Clarence and Rosannah Ethelton ” comes mainly from its high-concept premise: The title characters fall in love, quarrel, reconcile, and get married entirely over the phone, without ever meeting in person. At the time the story appeared, in March 1878, very few Americans had actually seen a telephone, and Twain plays up the strangeness of the new technology. When we are first introduced to Alonzo, in his study in Eastport, Maine, he seems to be talking to himself, or to someone in the next room, before it’s revealed that he’s actually on the phone with his Aunt Susan in San Francisco. But although Twain found technology fascinating, he also knew that things—even things that do amazing things—don’t make for good stories. The only subject that human beings find enduringly interesting is one another, and Twain was remarkably prescient about how the telephone would challenge traditional terms of interaction. The lovers in Twain’s story are separated by thousands of miles, but the conversation between them is not at either end, nor is it somewhere in the middle; it is a meeting of minds that have escaped the body’s requirement of place. This raises questions that we’re still asking today, in the age of dating apps and OnlyFans. Can people be real to one another without physical presence? Can there be love without touch? “There was a feeble but frantic sound for some little time, as if wool-lipped, disembodied spirits were exchanging kisses,” Twain writes about his telephone lovers. Is that funny or nightmarish? Gleick’s great achievement as a science writer has been to show how complicated, abstract ideas end up changing the way we experience the world. In Chaos , he explored chaos theory, which used new mathematical tools to explain why weather and other complex systems are so unpredictable. In The Information , he showed how modern discoveries such as DNA and the computer involved new ways of thinking about data and communication. The Telephone , too, is the story of a scientific discovery. But it’s just as much the history of a business—the Bell System, a group of companies led by the American Telephone and Telegraph Company (AT&T) that became America’s most powerful and enduring monopoly. The book is also a wide-ranging cultural history, showing how the telephone changed people’s lives and how they tried to make sense of those changes. When Bell gave a public demonstration of his invention in Salem, Massachusetts, speaking with Thomas Watson 18 miles away, in Boston, “it seemed as if an electric thrill went through the audience,” he remembered. “They recognized for the first time—what was meant by the ‘Telephone.’ ” But what did it mean, exactly? That is where novelists like Twain came in—along with playwrights, psychologists, social scientists, and legions of pundits in what Gleick calls the “Telephone Century.” Like artificial intelligence today, the telephone was an obviously momentous new technology that everyone had heard about and no one fully understood. If the parallel holds, we won’t know how AI is going to change the world until after it happens, because early predictions about how people would use the telephone turned out to be wildly off base. A New York Times article imagined it as a way to listen to sermons without having to go to church, joking that soon houses for rent would offer Baptist preachers “laid on in every room,” like hot and cold water. In France, the Théâtrophone service allowed subscribers (including Marcel Proust) to listen to live opera performances over the phone. In both cases, the telephone was viewed as a one-way delivery system. But its power would lie in being a network—literally, a web of metal cables spanning continents and oceans, which allowed any two people, anywhere in the world, to have a back-and-forth exchange. Not even Bell knew at first exactly what he was inventing. The initial goal of his research wasn’t to transmit the human voice, but to increase the carrying capacity of existing telegraph lines by sending multiple messages simultaneously at different pitches. In the course of his experiments with vibrating steel reeds, he discovered the principle that made the telephone possible: Sound and electricity speak the same language. Sound travels through the air in waves of pressure, and electromagnetic force also takes the form of a wave. The telephone was a tool for translating between the two kinds of waves. A small magnet, vibrating in response to a speaking voice, would generate an electrical current, which could be sent down a wire and reconverted into sound at the other end. Bell wasn’t the only person to make this discovery. Philipp Reis had built a device he called das Telephon in Germany in 1861, and Elisha Gray, an American inventor, was so close on Bell’s heels that both men’s applications reached the U.S. Patent Office on the same day. Bell was awarded the patent, as well as the chance to go down in history as the inventor of the telephone, mainly because his well-connected Washington lawyer bribed the patent examiner with $100 and a gold watch. Making the new invention useful would be a lot more expensive. As Gleick observes, other Industrial Age enterprises benefited from economies of scale. The more automobiles you make, the cheaper manufacturing each one becomes. With the telephone, the calculation was reversed: The bigger the network, the greater the cost per call, given how many lines and switchboards were required to put all the calls through. Raising capital from ultrarich investors became crucial. Originally Bell was one of four partners in the company that bore his name. Within three years, he had been reduced to one of 540 shareholders and ceased to play any real role. At first, independent telephone companies tried to challenge the Bell System, in business and in court. Some enterprising farmers even turned their barbed-wire fences into telephone lines by running electric current through them. But Bell’s patents gave AT&T an unbeatable head start, and it ruthlessly maintained its advantage for more than a century. Not until the case reached a federal appeals court, in 1956, did the company finally win the right to sell its $10 product. An antitrust suit led to the breakup of AT&T in 1984. By then, the telephone was so ubiquitous that its effect on modern life could hardly be grasped. Over a century, the meaning of distance had changed: The other side of the country, or the planet, didn’t seem so far away when you could communicate across it instantly, instead of waiting weeks to exchange letters. Privacy had become more accessible—teenagers could take the phone into their room, or a closet, and talk without a chaperone. But it was also more vulnerable.
